newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Conservative Harney gets top Irish job.
newsitem.headline: Conservative Harney gets top Irish job.

text.p: Mary Harney had big ambitions and a small party. She gave both to Fianna Fail leader Bertie Ahern and was on Thursday appointed his deputy Prime Minister.
It is the highest office a woman has reached in the male-dominated world of Irish politics, apart from the non-executive President's role held by Mary Robinson.
But for the mauling her Progressive Democrats took in the June 6 elections, Harney might also have been given a top ministerial portfolio of either Finance or Foreign Affairs.
The PDs, as they are known, retained only four of the eight seats they held before the June 6 election. Harney was appointed minister for Enterprise and Employment instead.
Throughout the election campaign she learned to curb her outspoken conservatism on issues ranging from payment of support to single mothers and civil service job cuts.

There was an outcry when she proposed stopping rent grants to single mothers to get them to go home. Her call for 25,000 job cuts in the civil service got an equally shrill reception, much of it from her Fianna Fail colleagues.
She did a prompt public U-turn on both subjects, not something she has a reputation for doing. Harney is admired by supporters and critics alike as a woman who speaks her mind.
It was speaking her mind that led to her splitting from Fianna Fail in 1985 to help found the party which is seen as right of centre, fiscally conservative and pro free-market.
A mould-breaker, Harney's political career began 20 years ago when she was nominated to the Irish Senate, the upper house of parliament, as its youngest ever member.
She was elected to the Dail, or lower house, for Fianna Fail in 1981 but broke with that party four years later to become a founding member of the Progressive Democrats.

The establishment of the new party, and its 1989 decision to enter coalition with Fianna Fail, are widely credited with breaking the mould in which Irish politics had been mired since the civil war of the 1920s.
In that 1989 coalition government, Harney became a junior minister at the Environment Ministry where her greatest achievement was solving Dublin's smog problem by banning the use of smoky coal.
Regarded as one of the best speakers in the Irish parliament, Harney's politics have been described as instinctive and populist rather than ideological.
Her pronouncements on issues such as standards in public life have struck a chord with voters and her personal rating with the electorate has remained consistently high.
"Her political judgement is sometimes faulty, frequently short-term but she possesses a journalist's eye for the right question and the good headline," one political commentator has said of her.
The Progressive Democrats are committed to cutting taxes, controlling spending and clamping down on crime, goals shared by Fianna Fail, the biggest party in Ireland.
They distinguish themselves from other political parties with their firm belief in privatisation, promising to use the proceeds to reduce Ireland's national debt.
"In the modern world, there is no rationale for state involvement in the running of hotels, fertiliser factories and other commercial enterprises," Harney has said.
They take a different tack on European economic and monetary union (EMU) as well, expressing reservations about Ireland joining a single currency without Britain.
On this, Harney is at odds with Fianna Fail, who are committed to joining the single currency in the first wave, with or without sterling.
